strengths: The paper targets an important practical problem: reducing the training cost of reinforcement learning for board games, where AlphaZero-style search-based training is expensive and difficult to reproduce.

The proposed KLENT update is simple and technically coherent: the closed-form policy improvement under reverse-KL and entropy regularization is clearly derived, and the use of lambda-returns for action-value learning is well motivated.

The empirical section is broader than many board-game RL papers, covering five games plus a 19x19 Go experiment, ablations for the three main components, hyperparameter sensitivity, rollout-count studies for AlphaZero, and test-time-search scaling.
The ablation results support the main design choices: removing entropy, removing KL regularization, or using pure 1-step/Monte Carlo targets consistently hurts at least some environments.
The paper is generally well written, with a clear limitations section acknowledging that the results concern efficiency rather than asymptotic superiority under very large compute budgets.
weaknesses: The novelty is modest. KL regularization, entropy regularization, lambda-returns, action-value heads, and self-play are all standard ingredients; the contribution is mainly an empirical combination rather than a substantially new algorithm or theory.

The central efficiency claim depends heavily on the chosen compute metric. Counting simulator evaluations/neural-network queries is informative, but it does not fully capture training cost, optimizer updates, batching, memory traffic, or wall-clock cost across model-free and MCTS-based methods. The appendix gives some inference-time timing, but training-time cost comparisons remain incomplete.

Baseline strength and tuning are a concern. PPO and DQN appear to use relatively generic Stable-Baselines-style hyperparameters, while AlphaZero-family methods rely on third-party implementations and mostly fixed settings in the main experiments. Although the appendices partially address AlphaZero rollout counts, the comparison would be more convincing with equally extensive tuning for all baselines and direct head-to-head tournaments among learned agents.

Evaluation against fixed anchored opponents from Pgx is useful but narrow. Win rate against one stochastic reference policy can obscure exploitability, cyclic dominance, or poor generalization to other opponents; Elo and head-to-head results are relegated to appendices and are still limited.

The scalability evidence is suggestive but not decisive. The 19x19 Go result shows competitiveness against an AlphaZero baseline under a fixed budget, but not against strong modern Go systems or well-tuned large-scale search-based training, so claims about large-scale board-game performance should remain cautious.

Reproducibility is only partial. The paper gives many implementation details, but several important details are unclear or missing, such as exact buffer capacities, number of update epochs per collection phase, loss weighting between policy and Q terms, illegal-action masking details, checkpoint selection, and whether code/checkpoints will be released. The reported total compute of about 2,000 A100 GPU hours may also limit independent verification.

The limitations and ethics discussion is minimal. There are no major ethical concerns for board-game RL, but the manuscript could better discuss environmental cost, reproducibility barriers from high compute, and the dependence on existing game simulators and baseline implementations.

strengths: The paper asks a relevant question: whether board-game RL can reduce reliance on expensive training-time search. This is practically meaningful because AlphaZero-style methods remain costly to reproduce.

KLENT is clearly described at the algorithmic level. The closed-form regularized policy update is derived, the training loop is specified, and the method combines recognizable ingredients: reverse KL regularization, entropy regularization, and lambda-returns.

The experimental scope is broader than many board-game RL papers, covering five medium-scale games plus an additional 19x19 Go experiment, ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity, rollout-count studies, and some head-to-head evaluations.
The limitations section is honest in noting that the work focuses on efficiency rather than asymptotic strength, and that search-based methods may remain preferable with very large compute budgets.
weaknesses: The central efficiency claim is not fully convincing. The main comparison uses simulator evaluations as the x-axis, but this is an imperfect proxy for compute across model-free and MCTS-based methods. Search methods consume simulator calls, neural-network evaluations, tree-management overhead, and fewer parameter updates in different proportions. The paper gives only limited wall-clock evidence and does not consistently use wall-clock, FLOPs, energy, or matched training-update budgets in the main results.

The baseline comparisons appear fragile. Main AlphaZero-family baselines use a fixed MCTS simulation budget of 32, while later appendices show performance is highly sensitive to rollout count. Rollout tuning is only explored for Go, not all five environments, so the claim of broad superiority over search-based methods may partly reflect under-tuned baselines.

The evaluation protocol relies heavily on win rate against fixed anchored opponents from Pgx or ElfOpenGo rather than a fuller round-robin or population-based evaluation. This can obscure non-transitive behavior and does not necessarily establish absolute playing strength or robust superiority over the baselines.

The novelty is modest. The method is a recombination of known regularized policy optimization ideas, entropy regularization, and lambda-returns. The paper acknowledges this, but the empirical evidence is not strong enough to elevate the contribution to a clear ICML-level advance.

The model-free framing is somewhat overstated. The paper contrasts KLENT with search-based training, but important supplementary evaluations and head-to-head results use test-time MCTS with KLENT parameters. This is not inherently invalid, but the narrative sometimes blurs training efficiency, no-search policy strength, and search-augmented strength.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The manuscript provides many implementation details, but I do not see a clear code-release statement, exact training schedules, buffer capacities, update-to-data ratios, and full baseline tuning procedures sufficient for reliable independent reproduction, especially given the large reported compute budget of about 2,000 A100 GPU hours.

The paper makes broad claims about applicability to discrete optimization, algorithmic discovery, and theorem proving, but evaluates only board games. These extrapolations are speculative and should be substantially toned down or experimentally supported.

Presentation is generally readable but sometimes overclaims from limited evidence. Important numerical results are often only in plots, and several decisive comparisons would benefit from tables, confidence intervals beyond three seeds, and clearer separation between main evidence and appendix-only support.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and practical question: whether board-game RL can be made substantially more resource-efficient by eliminating look-ahead search during training. This is a meaningful direction given the reproducibility and compute barriers of AlphaZero-style methods.

The proposed KLENT algorithm is simple, well motivated, and technically coherent. Combining reverse KL regularization, entropy regularization, and lambda-returns is not individually novel, but the paper gives a clear derivation of the closed-form policy target and a plausible algorithmic recipe for finite-action board games.

The empirical evaluation is broad for this problem class: five medium-scale board games plus an additional 19x19 Go experiment, comparisons to AlphaZero, TRPO AlphaZero, Gumbel AlphaZero, PPO, and DQN, and ablations for all three main components.

The ablation study is a real strength. It supports the claim that the particular combination of entropy, KL regularization, and intermediate lambda-returns matters, rather than the gains coming from a single obvious tweak.

The appendices add useful credibility: hyperparameter sensitivity, details on AlphaZero implementation reliability, rollout-count studies, larger-budget AlphaZero comparisons, test-time search scaling, and head-to-head Go evaluations against GnuGo/Pachi.

Presentation is generally clear. The paper states its limitation that KLENT is aimed at efficiency rather than superior asymptotic performance, and the method/experimental setup are described in enough detail to understand the main claims.
weaknesses: The originality is moderate. KLENT is mainly a careful recombination of known ingredients: KL-regularized policy optimization, entropy regularization, and lambda-return value learning. The contribution is mostly empirical, so acceptance depends heavily on whether the experimental comparison is judged convincing.

The main efficiency metric, simulator evaluations during training, is useful but incomplete. The paper does not provide a sufficiently direct wall-clock or energy-cost comparison for training, even though the central motivation is resource efficiency. Test-time wall-clock is discussed, but training-time compute accounting remains less satisfying.

The comparison to search-based methods is somewhat delicate. AlphaZero-family performance depends strongly on rollout counts, training schedule, implementation details, and hyperparameter tuning. The paper includes additional rollout studies, but these are mainly for Go and do not fully eliminate concern that some baselines may be under-optimized across all five environments.

The reported gains are strongest against anchored opponents and under fixed-budget learning curves, but the paper gives less evidence about absolute playing strength across broader opponent pools. Some results show win rates against fixed Pgx or ElfOpenGo anchors, which are useful but may not fully characterize strategic robustness.

The method still uses substantial compute, around 2,000 A100 GPU-hours for the main experiments, so the framing as resource-efficient should be interpreted relatively to AlphaZero-style training rather than as broadly low-cost or easily reproducible by small labs.

The 19x19 Go result is encouraging but not fully decisive: the paper reports competitive learning efficiency versus AlphaZero under a limited setup, but not a strong comparison to highly optimized modern Go systems or to extensively tuned search-based training at larger scale.

Reproducibility is decent but not complete from the manuscript alone. Many implementation details are provided, but full confidence depends on release of code, exact configurations, checkpoints, and plotting/evaluation scripts. The paper does not clearly state that all artifacts are already available.

The limitations and ethics discussion is minimal. Ethical concerns are low for board-game RL, but the paper could better discuss compute/environmental cost and possible overclaiming when extrapolating from games to domains such as theorem proving, algorithmic discovery, or discrete optimization.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical problem: reducing the cost of self-play reinforcement learning for two-player board games without relying on training-time search. The proposed KLENT algorithm is simple, well motivated, and connects naturally to regularized policy optimization.
weaknesses: The finite-length game convergence theorem is not fully convincing as stated. The proof assumes that action-value estimates converge after sufficiently many updates and then uses backward induction, but this largely bypasses the main difficulties of stochastic approximation, function approximation, self-play nonstationarity, finite sampling, and bootstrapped lambda-return learning. Thus the practical algorithm's convergence is not established by the theorem.

strengths: The paper studies a relevant problem: reducing the training cost of self-play agents for two-player games by avoiding MCTS during training. The proposed KLENT update is simple, computationally attractive, and clearly connected to known regularized policy optimization ideas.

The manuscript includes a reasonably broad empirical suite for board-game RL, covering Animal Shogi, Gardner Chess, 9x9 Go, Hex, Othello, and an additional 19x19 Go experiment. The ablations over KL regularization, entropy regularization, and lambda-returns are useful and suggest that the combination is practically important.

The appendix contains many implementation and evaluation details, including architecture descriptions, hyperparameter sensitivity for KLENT, additional model-free baselines, rollout-count studies for AlphaZero in 9x9 Go, and test-time MCTS experiments. This improves the paper’s reproducibility relative to many RL submissions.
The limitations section is honest that the contribution is about efficiency rather than asymptotic dominance, and the paper does not claim entirely new algorithmic ingredients.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is much weaker than the paper suggests. The normal-form result is only local convergence around a fixed point under a sufficient contraction condition, yet the main text phrases it as convergence to a unique fixed point without adequately proving uniqueness or global relevance. This does not support broad claims about stable self-play learning in board games.

The finite-length game theorem appears largely unsupported. The proof assumes that the action-value estimates converge after sufficiently many updates, then derives the policy limit. But this is the central difficulty of the algorithm, especially under sampling, bootstrapping/lambda-returns, function approximation, and nonstationary self-play. As written, the theorem is closer to a conditional fixed-point argument than a convergence proof for KLENT.

There is a substantial gap between the theory and the practical algorithm. The theory analyzes exact tabular-style updates or simplified games, while the experiments use neural networks, sampled actions, partial action-value supervision, lambda-returns, and alternating data collection/fitting. The manuscript does not establish that the theoretical stability mechanisms carry over to the implemented method.

The empirical comparison is not sufficiently convincing for the central claim of superiority over search-based methods. Main evaluations often use no search at test time, which is an unnatural setting for AlphaZero-family agents, while KLENT is designed for reactive play. The appendix adds test-time MCTS, but those results are limited and still rely heavily on anchored win rates rather than comprehensive head-to-head or tournament evaluation.

Baseline tuning and fairness are concerns. AlphaZero-family methods are mainly run through a particular Pgx/Mctx implementation, with 32 rollouts in the main experiments, while appendix tuning shows that different rollout counts can materially change results. The tuning appears much more extensive for KLENT than for all baselines and is not consistently repeated across all games.

The compute metric of simulator evaluations is incomplete. KLENT and AlphaZero-family methods have different numbers of neural-network evaluations, update schedules, action-value/policy heads, and wall-clock profiles. The paper claims efficiency, but wall-clock training comparisons are limited and do not fully substantiate the several-fold efficiency claims across environments.

Several experimental results are less strong than the narrative implies. KLENT is only competitive in some low-branching games, Othello gains are modest, and in test-time MCTS Animal Shogi KLENT is below Gumbel AlphaZero. The average curves obscure these mixed outcomes.

The model-free baselines are not persuasive. DQN/PPO/GRPO/Munchausen comparisons appear to use generic settings or lightly adapted implementations; poor performance of these baselines does not establish that KLENT is uniquely effective unless comparable tuning effort is demonstrated.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite many details. The manuscript does not clearly state that code and exact training scripts/checkpoints will be released, and the experiments require roughly 2000 A100 GPU-hours, making independent verification difficult.

Presentation has notable issues: some appendix text appears to refer to a reviewer question, which is inappropriate for an anonymous main-track submission; there are grammatical problems throughout; and some figures are hard to interpret quantitatively because exact values and uncertainty are mostly not tabulated in the main paper.

The impact statement is boilerplate and does not meaningfully discuss possible dual-use or societal implications of stronger, cheaper game/search agents, even though the introduction explicitly connects the method to algorithmic discovery and mathematical proving.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely question: whether self-play board-game learning can be made competitive without training-time tree search. The proposed KLENT algorithm is simple, well motivated by reverse-KL and entropy regularized policy optimization, and practically appealing because it directly learns policy and action-value heads rather than relying on MCTS targets.

The empirical evaluation is broad and substantially stronger than average for this area. Results cover five board games, a 19x19 Go experiment, ablations for KL regularization, entropy regularization, and lambda-returns, hyperparameter sensitivity, architecture variants, additional model-free baselines, rollout-count tuning for AlphaZero, larger AlphaZero training budgets, and test-time MCTS scaling. The main efficiency claim is therefore supported by multiple angles rather than a single benchmark curve.

The paper is honest about the nature of the contribution: it does not oversell new algorithmic ingredients, but argues that this particular combination has useful theoretical and empirical behavior in two-player games. This framing improves credibility and helps position the work relative to AlphaZero-style and regularized-RL methods.

The normal-form-game analysis provides a clean local convergence condition and improves over a cited prior sufficient condition. The synthetic matching-pennies and count-up experiments are useful sanity checks that connect the theory to the proposed update rule.

Presentation is generally clear. The algorithm is easy to understand, figures and tables communicate the main findings effectively, and the appendices include many details needed to interpret the results, including seeds, evaluation protocols, architectures, hyperparameters, and compute usage.

Reproducibility is reasonably good for a large-scale RL paper: the authors use public environments/implementations where possible, specify network and optimizer details, report three seeds for the main curves, use 1024-game evaluations, and discuss the reliability of the AlphaZero baseline implementation.
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantees are narrower and less formal than the main text may suggest. The normal-form result is local, depends on a fixed point, and the claimed uniqueness is not fully established in the main theorem statement. The finite-length-game convergence proof appears to assume convergence of learned action-value estimates and effectively sidesteps the harder issues introduced by sampling, bootstrapping, nonstationary self-play, and function approximation. Thus the theory supports the update intuition, but not the full practical deep RL algorithm.

The empirical comparisons use simulator evaluations as the primary training-cost metric, which is reasonable and common, but not a complete compute measure. KLENT trains an action-value head and stores improved policies, while search methods trade simulator calls for MCTS structure; the paper gives some wall-clock evidence, but the main claims would be stronger with systematic wall-clock and hardware-normalized training comparisons across all games.

The asymptotic-performance question remains open. The paper acknowledges this limitation, and Appendix L shows AlphaZero can catch up in 9x9 Go with much larger budgets. This does not undermine the efficiency contribution, but it narrows the claim to fixed-budget learning rather than dominance as a game-playing method.

The baselines are strong and numerous, but some model-free baselines may be sensitive to tuning. PPO, DQN, SAC-style, MPO-style, Munchausen DQN, and GRPO underperform dramatically; without equally extensive tuning details for these methods, some of these negative comparisons should be interpreted cautiously.

Originality is moderate rather than exceptional. Reverse-KL regularization, entropy regularization, lambda-returns, action-value learning, and self-play are all established; the novelty lies in the careful combination, analysis, and empirical demonstration in board games. That is valuable, but not a fundamentally new algorithmic paradigm.

The impact statement is minimal. The work has no obvious acute ethical risk, but a more thoughtful discussion of compute, reproducibility barriers, and possible downstream use in automated search/planning systems would be preferable for a main-track submission.
